segments: There's a bird that does exactly one thing.
It does that thing better than we do anything.
You could take it anywhere — box it,
drive it five hundred miles in a
covered truck to a field it has never seen —
and the moment you open
the lid, it flies home.
Not toward home.
Home.
One loft, one perch, one door.
Nobody fully understands how,
and we have tried: magnetic fields,
the position of the sun,
the smell of the air,
even the routes of motorways.
The pigeon has declined to comment.
It just goes.
That's the entire animal — a heart,
two wings, and a forwarding address.
Hold on to that fact,
because everything you're about to
hear is built on top of it.
When a creature does one thing perfectly,
we don't leave it alone to enjoy it.
We give it a job.
The first job we gave it was war,
because a homing pigeon is a message
that can't be jammed,
intercepted, or reasoned with.
October 1918, the Argonne forest.
An American battalion is cut off, surrounded,
and being shelled by its own artillery.
The radios are gone and the runners are dead.
They're down to one last bird,
a pigeon named Cher Ami.
Cher Ami goes up through the gunfire,
takes a wound, and keeps flying —
roughly twenty-five miles back to the loft.
The shelling stops.
Around a hundred and ninety-four men
walk out of that forest alive.
France gave that bird the Croix de Guerre —
an actual military decoration,
pinned on a pigeon.
We keep it in the Smithsonian today.
And this is not a one-off.
Britain's Dickin Medal,
the animals' Victoria Cross,
has gone to pigeons thirty-two times.
Dogs have eighteen, horses three,
and — presumably over some objection —
there's one cat.
The all-time scoreboard of animal
bravery is pigeons, in a landslide.
Then the wars ended,
but the birds didn't,
and neither did the men
who'd learned to depend on them.
So we did the obvious thing:
we started racing them.
Here's how a pigeon race works,
and it's stranger than you'd think.
The birds are basketed
and driven away in a truck —
sixty kilometres for a sprint,
up to twelve hundred for the long hauls —
then released together in
one great clap of wings.
And then the race immediately disappears,
because every bird is flying to its own loft.
Your bird finishes at your house,
and your rival's bird finishes at his.
Nobody sees the middle.
There's no finish line, no stadium, no crowd —
just a sky full of athletes,
each running a private race home.
Therefore we score it the only way we can:
velocity, in yards per minute,
distance over time.
And because the moment there's a race
there's a man thinking about the result,
every bird carries a rubber ring
stamped with a secret number.
The ring is logged into a sealed
clock the owner can't open,
and these days it's an RFID chip.
Notice what that says about us.
The sport always trusted the bird completely.
The tamper-proofing was for us.
Now, a race decided by velocity becomes,
one generation later,
a race decided by breeding —
and the man who saw what pigeon
breeding really was happened to be
Charles Darwin.
On the Origin of Species, the book,
does not open with finches.
It opens with pigeon breeding.
Darwin kept a loft of his
own at his house in Kent.
He joined two London pigeon clubs —
one for gentlemen, one very much not —
and he attended both,
because on the subject of pigeons,
class did not apply.
Fanciers had been bending these birds
into new shapes for centuries before
we had a word for it.
Darwin just wrote down what the hobby proved.
And where breeding goes,
bloodlines follow,
and where bloodlines go,
our money follows.
November 2020,
a Belgian auction house called PIPA.
On the block is New Kim —
a two-year-old Belgian hen with a
fine racing career behind her and a
finer pedigree underneath it.
Two anonymous bidders take her to the
wire under the pseudonyms
Super Duper and Hitman —
grown adults, you understand,
moving actual fortunes under the
names of cartoon henchmen.
In the final half hour alone they add
two hundred and eighty thousand euros.
New Kim sells for one
point six million euros —
about one point nine
million dollars, for a pigeon.
That breaks the record set only the
year before by a cock named Armando.
And here's the detail you should keep.
New Kim was not bought to race.
She was bought to breed.
The most expensive bird on Earth was
purchased so she would
never have to go anywhere again.
Of course, once your bird
costs more than your house,
somebody somewhere wants an edge.
And in 2013 the Belgian federation
went looking for one.
They collected about twenty samples
from racing pigeons and anonymised them.
Here's the first twist:
their own tests found nothing.
So they shipped the droppings to a
laboratory in South Africa —
a lab whose regular day job is
testing racehorses.
Which means there was a morning when
some of the finest equine forensic
scientists on Earth arrived at work
to a parcel of Belgian pigeon droppings.
Six samples came back positive:
five for a painkiller made for humans,
and one for cocaine.
Somewhere in Belgium,
a pigeon had done cocaine.
And because the samples were anonymous,
that's the whole story —
six positives, zero names,
nobody punished.
The test could prove that doping existed;
it couldn't prove that anyone had doped.
The sport nodded at the result and carried on,
and so, if we're honest, did we.
But a drug only makes a bird a little
faster, and once we've made the prizes big
enough, a little stops being enough.
Shanghai, 2018.
Two racers, surnamed Gong and Zhang,
enter the city association's annual race —
roughly six hundred kilometres,
Henan province to Shanghai.
Their preparation takes a year,
which is longer than you'd spend
planning most honest things.
They raise their birds at two feeding points,
one in Henan and one in Shanghai,
so the pigeons grow up
treating both places as home.
Remember the one fact we started with:
a bird that knows exactly where home is.
If you wanted to beat a pigeon,
you would have to beat the only thing
it is ever certain about.
So the perfect fraud,
if you think it through,
is to give the bird a second home.
On race day they let the birds fly to
a spot near the start,
pack them into milk cartons —
milk cartons — and carry them to
Shanghai on a high-speed train.
They take the top four prizes,
worth over a million yuan —
about a hundred and fifty thousand dollars.
And they're caught because —
you can probably see this coming —
their birds are too fast.
The winning times shatter the race record,
because pigeons on a high-speed train
are very fast pigeons.
The sport looked at those times and knew.
And we should be fair
about what they were chasing,
because we are the ones who made a
bird worth a year of a man's life.
To cover it up, the two
men killed the birds and
returned the prize money.
A Shanghai court gave both of them
three-year suspended
sentences for fraud, and fined them.
They never cheated the clock;
the clock worked perfectly.
They cheated the bird's definition of home —
the one thing you would have sworn
could not be faked.
Which brings us to the joke sitting
underneath all of it —
the auctions, the pseudonyms,
the forensics, the milk cartons.
There has always been something
faster than cocaine —
faster, even, than the train —
and it's perfectly legal,
and every fancier knows it.
It's called the widowhood method,
and it works like this.
You pair a cock with a hen,
and you let them bond — nest, court,
settle into the small routines of a
married couple.
Then, on race day,
you take him away from her.
You basket him with the rest of the field,
you drive him three hundred miles,
and you open the door.
And he comes home like the sky is on fire,
because his mate is in that loft and
he doesn't know why he was taken from her —
only that every wingbeat closes the distance.
So look at the ledger
we've written for ourselves.
Giving a pigeon cocaine: banned.
Taking a pigeon's wife: technique.
That's the kind of rule we're
supposed to keep unwritten,
and the sport didn't even hide it —
it named the breakage
widowhood, which is both an
exaggeration and a confession.
The million-euro hen, the horse lab,
Super Duper and Hitman,
the sealed clocks —
all of it runs on a bird that wants,
more than anything,
to get back to his wife.
We built an economy on top of a marriage.
Which might explain why the people
who love these birds
love them the way they do —
completely, and a little past reason.
Mike Tyson's first fight,
before the belts, before any ring,
was a street fight in Brooklyn over a pigeon.
And he said it plainly years later:
the first thing he ever loved in his
life was a pigeon.
Because for all the money we've
stacked on this bird,
it has never once changed its terms.
It flew home through the guns of the Argonne.
It flew home past our rubber rings
and our sealed clocks.
It'll fly home tomorrow,
straight past whatever price we've put on it,
to one loft, one perch, one door.
We invented the sport, the market,
and the scandal;
the bird only ever invented one move.
It goes home.
Honestly — it's a pretty good move.
And it leaves us the fancier's job,
which turns out to be the only job in
the whole sport worth having,
and one you already know how to do.
Stand in your yard.
Watch your sky.
And when the dot appears —
when the one thing that always comes
back to you comes back to you — be glad.
